title: Playwright end-to-end tests that don't flake
objectives: Write locators in Playwright's recommended order — `getByRole` with an accessible name first, `getByTestId` as the fallback — and fix a strict-mode violation
Replace `waitForTimeout` and `expect(await locator.isVisible())` with auto-waiting actions and web-first assertions
Configure `webServer`, and explain how `reuseExistingServer` can run the suite against a different app already on the port
Diagnose flake — clicking before hydration, shared state, non-retrying assertions — and debug it with retries, traces and `--repeat-each`
Reuse a signed-in state with a setup project and `storageState`, and share setup through fixtures

sources.title: Next.js docs: Local development (next dev compiles on demand)

questions.prompt: Which locator does Playwright recommend for a row's "Delete" button?

options.text: `page.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete" })`
`page.locator(".btn-danger")`
`page.locator("//tr[3]/td[4]/button")`
`page.getByTestId("delete-button")`

questions.explanation: `getByRole` is first in Playwright's list because it matches how users and assistive technology see the page — a button named "Delete". A class is styling and an XPath is document structure; both change without the user noticing, which the docs call non-resilient. `getByTestId` works, but it's the fallback for when nothing a user can see identifies the element.

questions.prompt: `page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click()` throws `strict mode violation … resolved to 2 elements`. What's the best fix?

options.text: Scope the locator to the region that matters, e.g. `page.getByRole("dialog").getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })`
Add `.first()`
Pass `{ force: true }` to `click()`
Add `waitForTimeout(500)` so one of them disappears

questions.explanation: Strictness is Playwright refusing to guess which button you meant. Narrowing to the dialog (or giving the buttons distinct accessible names) says which one a user would press. `.first()` silences the error by picking by DOM order, which changes with layout. `force` only skips actionability checks, and sleeping doesn't make the locator unambiguous.

questions.prompt: "Saved" appears 800 ms after clicking Save. `expect(await page.getByText("Saved").isVisible()).toBe(true)` fails immediately. Why?

options.text: `isVisible()` answers once, right now, and hands `expect` a plain boolean; use `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`, which retries
The default 5 s assertion timeout is too short
`isVisible()` must not be awaited
`getByText` can't find text inside a toast

questions.explanation: Only web-first assertions (`expect(locator).toBeVisible()`, `toHaveText`, …) re-check the page until the condition holds. `isVisible()` is a one-off read; by the time `expect` sees `false`, there's nothing left to retry. The 5 s default would be plenty — it just never applied to a boolean.

questions.prompt: A suite uses `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)` before its assertions and currently passes. What's wrong with it?

options.text: It's a race against machine speed — too short on a slow CI run, wasted time everywhere else; wait for the condition instead
Nothing, as long as it passes
`waitForTimeout` was removed in Playwright 1.6x
It blocks every parallel worker for a second

questions.explanation: Playwright marks `waitForTimeout` Discouraged: tests that wait for time are inherently flaky. A fixed sleep guesses how long something takes; a web-first assertion waits exactly as long as needed and fails with a useful message if it never happens. It still exists, and it only pauses its own test.

questions.prompt: Locally, `reuseExistingServer: true` and `url: "http://localhost:3000"`. A trace shows a page from a *different* project. What happened?

options.text: Another project's dev server was already on :3000; Playwright saw the URL answer and reused it without checking which app it was
The browser served a cached page from an earlier run
`baseURL` was ignored because `webServer` was set
`reuseExistingServer` only works in CI

questions.explanation: "Available" means the URL answered with an accepted status (2xx, 3xx, 400–403) — nothing checks identity. Your command never ran. Give each project its own port, use a readiness URL only your app serves (e.g. `/api/health`, which another app would 404, so Playwright tries to start yours and fails loudly on the busy port), and keep `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI`.

questions.prompt: Under `next dev`, a test fills the "New todo" field and clicks Add right after `goto`. The URL becomes `/todos?title=Buy+milk` and no todo is added. Why?

options.text: The click landed before React hydrated, so the browser submitted the plain HTML form as a GET instead of running `onSubmit`
Playwright clicked before the button was visible
The server rejected the POST and redirected
The locator matched two buttons and Playwright clicked the wrong one

questions.explanation: The server-rendered button is visible, enabled and stable before any JavaScript runs, so Playwright's actionability checks pass. Until hydration attaches the handler that calls `preventDefault()`, the form does what HTML forms do: GET its URL with the fields as a query string. Wait for a hydration signal (or test a production build, where hydration is quicker) before interacting.

options.text: It holds a live session — cookies and headers that could impersonate the test account
It's too large to commit
Playwright refuses to read a committed state file
It's a binary file that breaks diffs

questions.explanation: `storageState` writes cookies and local storage to disk — a working login. Playwright's docs strongly discourage committing it to any repository, public or private. The setup project rewrites it before each run anyway, so nothing is lost by ignoring it.

questions.prompt: With `retries: 2`, a test fails, then passes on retry, and the report marks it **flaky**. What should you do?

options.text: Treat it as a bug: open the retry's trace, and reproduce with `--repeat-each`
Nothing — it passed in the end
Raise `retries` to 5 so it passes more reliably
Add a `waitForTimeout` before the failing step

questions.explanation: Playwright reports "flaky" separately from passed precisely so it isn't mistaken for green: something in the test or the app is nondeterministic. `trace: "on-first-retry"` captures what differed, and `--repeat-each=20` makes a 1-in-20 failure show up locally. More retries and sleeps hide the race; they don't remove it.

prompts.prompt: Click the button by role and name, then assert with a web-first assertion that waits for the list.
prompts.explanation: `getByRole` plus the accessible name is the recommended first choice. Web-first assertions are async and retry until they pass, so they must be awaited — without `await`, the test can finish before the check runs.

prompts.prompt: Reuse an already-running dev server locally, but always start a fresh one in CI.
prompts.explanation: That's the value Playwright's docs recommend. In CI nothing should already be listening, so an occupied port fails loudly instead of being reused. The `/api/health` readiness URL adds a second guard: another app on the port would answer it with a 404.

prompts.prompt: Record a trace only when a failed test is retried.
prompts.explanation: Passing runs stay cheap, and every failure that gets retried leaves a trace — DOM snapshots per action, console and network — that you open with `npx playwright show-report` or `npx playwright show-trace`.

prompts.prompt: Save the signed-in state in the setup test, and make the browser project wait for setup.
prompts.explanation: `context().storageState({ path })` writes cookies and local storage to a file; the project's `use.storageState` loads it into every test's fresh context. `dependencies` makes the setup project run first.

prompts.prompt: Define a fixture that opens the todo page; the test runs where the fixture hands control over.
code: export const test = base.___<{ todoPage: TodoPage }>({
prompts.explanation: `test.extend` returns a new `test` with the fixture available by name. Code before `use(...)` is setup, code after it is teardown — and it runs even when the test fails, and only for tests that ask for `todoPage`.

code: webServer: { command: "PORT=4610 node my-app.mjs", url: "http://localhost:4610", reuseExistingServer: true }
// Before the run, another project's server is already listening on :4610,
snippets.question: What happens when you run the test?
snippets.answer: It fails: Expected "My Todos", Received "Some Other Project"
acceptable: it fails against the other app
snippets.explanation: Playwright saw the URL answer, reused the server, and never ran `my-app.mjs` — the test ran against the other project. A heading check made it visible; a status-only check would have passed. With `reuseExistingServer: false` the run stops before any test with "http://localhost:4610 is already used".

code: // The onSubmit handler (preventDefault + add item) attaches only after hydration,
snippets.question: What URL is printed (baseURL `http://localhost:4610`)?
snippets.explanation: Playwright's checks passed — the button was visible, enabled and stable in the server HTML — so it clicked at once. No handler existed yet, so the browser submitted the form natively: a GET with the field in the query string, and a full page load instead of a new todo. Waiting for a hydration signal first keeps the URL at `/todos`.

snippets.question: Which test passes?
snippets.answer: D passes; C fails at once with Expected: true, Received: false
snippets.explanation: C reads visibility once, immediately after load, before the text exists. D's web-first assertion re-checks until the text appears (within the 5 s default) and passes after about 800 ms.
